title: Inequalities, Bounds & Optimization
coreInsight: Many problems ask for a range of feasible values or an extreme feasible value rather than one exact equality.
targetLearnerRealization: An inequality describes a whole feasible region, and optimization means choosing an extreme value that still lies inside that region.
learningObjectives: Translate at least, at most, greater than, and less than conditions into inequalities.
Represent feasible values on a number line with correct open or closed endpoints.
Solve one-variable linear inequalities while reversing the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Apply integer restrictions after solving an inequality.
Find a requested minimum or maximum only after establishing feasibility.

continuity.openingCallback: Compare the single value that makes x + 7 = 18 true with all values that make x + 7 ≤ 18 true.
closingSeeds: A constraint can leave an interval of feasible values instead of one answer.
Several constraints can trim a feasible region before an extreme is chosen.
With two varying quantities, the feasible set can become a region of ordered pairs.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: An inequality has one numerical answer.
Equation rules can be copied blindly when multiplying or dividing by negatives.

beats.purpose: Turn a familiar one-value equation into a many-value capacity constraint.
beats.expectedRealization: Several values can satisfy one inequality.
beats.transitionIn: The equation x + 7 = 18 has one solution. Change “equals 18” to “is at most 18,” and the question changes shape.
beats.prompt: A bin holds at most 18 kilograms and already contains 7 kilograms. Which amounts x could be added? Select every amount that works.

data.label: Possible added mass x, in kilograms

visual.ariaLabel: An unshaded number line from zero to eighteen kilograms

response.feedback: Add each proposed amount to the 7 kilograms already in the bin.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Every selected value keeps the total at or below 18 kilograms.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Test each amount in 7 + x ≤ 18. More than one value works, but the total may not exceed 18.

visual.ariaLabel: The allowed interval from zero through eleven kilograms, including both endpoints

steps.title: Find the boundary
steps.body: The capacity rule is 7 + x ≤ 18. Subtracting 7 from both sides gives x ≤ 11.

steps.title: Keep the physical condition
steps.body: An added mass cannot be negative, so every value from 0 through 11 is feasible.

resolution.takeaway: An inequality can describe a whole interval of solutions, not just one number.

beats.purpose: Connect verbal boundary language to the correct inequality symbol.
beats.expectedRealization: At most includes the boundary and allows every smaller value.
beats.transitionIn: The shaded interval came from one phrase: “at most 18 kilograms.” Record that phrase symbolically.
beats.prompt: Which statement says that 7 kilograms plus x kilograms may equal 18 but may not exceed it?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The symbol ≤ keeps 18 available while excluding totals above it.
beats.incorrectFeedback: “At most” points toward smaller totals and includes the stated boundary.

steps.title: Read both parts of the symbol
steps.body: The < part says the total may be smaller than 18; the added bar says equality at 18 is also allowed.

resolution.takeaway: At most means ≤; at least means ≥.

beats.purpose: Make endpoint inclusion a mathematical decision rather than a drawing convention.
beats.expectedRealization: A strict inequality excludes its boundary and uses an open endpoint.
beats.transitionIn: The bar under ≤ admitted the boundary. Remove that bar and test the boundary again.
beats.prompt: A room must contain fewer than 40 people. Which statement about the boundary value 40 is correct?

options.text: 40 is allowed, so the endpoint is closed.
40 is not allowed, so the endpoint is open.
The phrase gives no information about 40.

beats.correctFeedback: Right. “Fewer than 40” means p < 40, so 40 is excluded.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Substitute p = 40 into the phrase “fewer than 40” and decide whether it is true.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line shaded from zero through values below forty, closed at zero and open at forty

steps.title: Test the boundary
steps.body: The sentence p < 40 is false when p = 40, so the mark at 40 stays open.

resolution.takeaway: Use a closed endpoint for ≤ or ≥ and an open endpoint for < or >.

beats.purpose: Extend equality-preserving moves to an inequality with a positive coefficient.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding, subtracting, or dividing by a positive number preserves the inequality direction.
beats.transitionIn: Endpoints record the final bound. Reach that bound with the same matched operations used for equations.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Subtract 4, then divide by positive 3; all values at or below 5 remain allowed.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Apply each operation to both sides: first subtract 4, then divide both sides by positive 3.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line shaded left without bound through a closed endpoint at five

steps.title: Subtract equally
steps.body: 3x + 4 ≤ 19 becomes 3x ≤ 15 after subtracting 4 from both sides.

steps.title: Divide by a positive number
steps.body: Dividing both sides by 3 gives x ≤ 5. The order direction stays the same.

resolution.takeaway: The familiar equation moves still work; the result is an interval rather than one value.

beats.purpose: Surface and repair blind copying of the inequality direction through division by a negative.
beats.expectedRealization: Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses order, so the inequality symbol must reverse.
beats.transitionIn: Positive division preserved the order. A negative divisor changes which side contains the greater numbers.
beats.prompt: Solve -2x < 6. Which result survives a check with x = 0?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Zero makes the original inequality true and lies in x > -3.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The test value x = 0 gives 0 < 6, so the final interval must contain 0. Dividing by -2 reverses order.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line with an open endpoint at negative three and shading to the right without bound

steps.title: Watch the order reverse
steps.body: Dividing -2x < 6 by -2 changes x's side from the smaller product to the greater quotient, giving x > -3.

steps.title: Check values on both sides
steps.body: x = 0 works because 0 < 6. But x = -4 fails because 8 < 6 is false.

resolution.takeaway: Reverse the inequality direction whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number.

beats.purpose: Name inequalities, bounds, feasible values, and optimization after learners have encountered each need.
beats.expectedRealization: Solving finds the feasible set; optimizing selects an extreme within it.
beats.name: Feasible intervals and extreme values
beats.conciseDefinition: An inequality compares quantities and describes all values that make the comparison true. Those values are feasible. Optimization asks for the greatest or least feasible value.
beats.formalization: solve the constraints → mark the feasible set → apply whole-number or other restrictions → choose the requested extreme

beats.purpose: Use a clean budget constraint to separate solving an interval from maximizing over whole numbers.
beats.expectedRealization: The inequality yields several feasible counts, while the word greatest selects one boundary count.
beats.transitionIn: A budget is another upper bound. First find every whole-number ticket count that fits; only then answer “greatest.”
beats.whyNow: The learner has built and transformed intervals and is ready to distinguish the feasible set from its maximum.
beats.entryBridge: Let t be a nonnegative whole number of ride tickets and keep admission inside the total cost.
beats.exitBridge: The boundary count fits exactly, while the next whole number crosses the budget.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A closed whole-number interval ending at the greatest affordable count.
learnerPrompts: Which inequality describes the budget, and which feasible whole number lies farthest to the right?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The feasible counts are 0 through 6, so the greatest is 6.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract the 16-dollar admission first, divide the remaining budget by 7, and check the next whole ticket count.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line shaded from zero through six, including both endpoints

steps.title: Solve the budget constraint
steps.body: 16 + 7t ≤ 58 gives 7t ≤ 42, then t ≤ 6.

steps.title: Apply the counting restriction
steps.body: Ticket counts are nonnegative whole numbers, so the feasible set is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

steps.title: Optimize and verify
steps.body: The greatest feasible count is 6. It costs 16 + 7(6) = 58 dollars; 7 tickets would cost 65 dollars.

resolution.takeaway: The inequality answers what is feasible; “greatest” chooses the rightmost feasible whole number.

beats.purpose: Make the two logical stages of optimization explicit and correctly ordered.
beats.expectedRealization: A single optimum is justified only after the complete feasible set is known.
beats.transitionIn: Six answered the festival question, but 0 through 5 also obeyed the budget. Separate those two facts.
beats.prompt: Which explanation correctly separates feasibility from optimization?

options.text: Feasibility gives 0 through 6; optimization then selects 6 as greatest.
Feasibility gives only 6 because smaller counts do not spend the full budget.
Optimization gives 0 through 6; feasibility then selects 6.
Optimization should compare 6 with 7 even though 7 exceeds the budget.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Feasibility produces the set; optimization selects one edge of it.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First identify every count that obeys the budget, then use “greatest” to choose from that set.

steps.title: Keep the jobs distinct
steps.body: The constraint proves why 0 through 6 are allowed. The optimization word greatest then selects 6 from those allowed counts.

resolution.takeaway: Never optimize over values before proving that they are feasible.

beats.purpose: Apply constraint-first optimization to a structural contest problem where the tempting unconstrained minimum is invalid.
beats.expectedRealization: The fewest blocks per isolated row is not the wall optimum because adjacent rows must also satisfy staggering.
beats.transitionIn: A budget ruled out ticket counts that were too large. In this wall, a construction rule rules out the tempting smallest count.
beats.whyNow: The learner can distinguish feasibility from optimization; the wall tests that distinction without requiring formal inequality notation for every construction rule.
beats.entryBridge: Treat each candidate wall as feasible only if it is 100 feet long, 7 feet high, even at both ends, and has staggered vertical joins.
beats.exitBridge: The minimum comes from the smallest surviving row pattern, alternated enough times to satisfy every join constraint.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Candidate counts are rejected by constraints before the smallest survivor is chosen.
learnerPrompts: Why is 50 the fewest blocks for one 100-foot row?
Which staggering constraint makes seven copies of that row infeasible?
Why does a shifted row require 51 blocks?
Among feasible seven-row arrangements, why is 353 minimal?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Four 50-block rows and three shifted 51-block rows give the smallest feasible total, 353.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Check the staggering rule before minimizing. Adjacent rows cannot use the same vertical join locations.

steps.title: Find the unconstrained row minimum
steps.body: A 100-foot row needs at least 100 ÷ 2 = 50 blocks, achieved by using only 2-foot blocks.

steps.title: Reject the repeated-row trap
steps.body: If every row uses that same pattern, all vertical joins line up. The wall is not feasible.

steps.title: Build the cheapest shifted row
steps.body: A 1-foot block at each end shifts the joins; 49 two-foot blocks fill the middle. That row uses 1 + 49 + 1 = 51 blocks.

steps.title: Optimize among feasible walls
steps.body: Alternation allows at most four 50-block rows among seven rows, so the minimum is 4(50) + 3(51) = 353 blocks.

resolution.takeaway: A smaller-looking candidate is irrelevant if it violates a constraint; optimize only among survivors.

beats.purpose: Assess an inclusive upper bound and maximum whole-number count.
beats.whyNow: Return to a clean capacity setting after the layered wall constraint.
beats.entryBridge: Translate “at most” before choosing the greatest full-jug count.
beats.exitBridge: The boundary count is safe exactly; the next count is not.
learnerPrompts: Which inequality bounds the full-jug count, and does equality at 40 liters count?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Nine jugs reach 40 liters exactly, so 9 is the greatest safe count.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Solve 13 + 3j ≤ 40, then test the boundary count and the next whole number.

steps.title: Find the feasible counts
steps.body: 13 + 3j ≤ 40 gives j ≤ 9.

steps.title: Choose the maximum
steps.body: Nine jugs give 40 liters and ten give 43, so 9 is greatest.

resolution.takeaway: An inclusive capacity can make equality the optimal boundary.

beats.purpose: Assess reversal under negative division and selection of a minimum integer.
beats.whyNow: The next constraint is symbolic and tests whether order is preserved correctly.
beats.entryBridge: Keep the endpoint included, but watch what dividing by -4 does to the direction.
beats.exitBridge: Substitution confirms both the reversed direction and the included endpoint.
learnerPrompts: After isolating -4x, which direction must the inequality face?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The solution is x ≥ -4, whose smallest integer is -4.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract 3, then reverse the inequality when dividing both sides by -4.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line with a closed endpoint at negative four and shading to the right

steps.title: Reverse on negative division
steps.body: -4x + 3 ≤ 19 becomes -4x ≤ 16, then x ≥ -4.

steps.title: Check the requested extreme
steps.body: At x = -4, the left side equals 19. Smaller integers fail, so -4 is the minimum.

resolution.takeaway: The reversed inequality determines which endpoint can be the minimum.

beats.purpose: Assess strict endpoint exclusion under a whole-number recording rule.
beats.whyNow: Change an inclusive capacity into a strict performance boundary.
beats.entryBridge: Decide whether 52 itself belongs before choosing the greatest whole number.
beats.exitBridge: The open endpoint removes 52, leaving 51 as the nearest feasible integer.
learnerPrompts: What does “less than 52” do to the endpoint?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Since 52 is excluded, 51 is the greatest qualifying whole-number time.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The word “less” is strict: exclude 52, then use the whole-number recording rule.

steps.title: Exclude the boundary
steps.body: The rule is t < 52, so 52 does not qualify.

steps.title: Use integer feasibility
steps.body: The greatest whole number below 52 is 51.

resolution.takeaway: An open endpoint can move a whole-number optimum one step inward.

beats.purpose: Assess an inclusive lower bound and least feasible whole-number count.
beats.whyNow: Reverse the optimization direction from a maximum under a cap to a minimum needed for a goal.
beats.entryBridge: “At least” points toward counts large enough to reach the goal; choose the leftmost feasible whole number.
beats.exitBridge: Eight reaches the boundary exactly, while seven remains short.
learnerPrompts: Which lower-bound inequality represents the goal, and which feasible whole number is least?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Eight boxes reach 125 books exactly; seven are not enough.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Solve 37 + 11b ≥ 125, then compare the smallest candidate with the whole number just below it.

steps.title: Choose the minimum
steps.body: Eight boxes reach 125; seven reach only 114. The least feasible count is 8.

resolution.takeaway: For an at-least goal, the optimum is often the leftmost feasible whole number.

beats.purpose: Assess multi-step constrained optimization with geometry and integer side lengths.
beats.whyNow: Finish with an objective that must be computed after a separate perimeter constraint is solved.
beats.entryBridge: Use the perimeter to bound the width before calculating any candidate area.
beats.exitBridge: The greatest feasible width produces the greatest area because the length grows with it.
learnerPrompts: What is the greatest feasible width, and why does it also maximize w(w + 3)?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Width 10 and length 13 meet the perimeter limit and give area 130.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Write 2w + 2(w + 3) ≤ 46, find the greatest whole-number width, and only then compute area.

steps.title: Bound the width
steps.body: 2w + 2(w + 3) ≤ 46 simplifies to 4w + 6 ≤ 46, so w ≤ 10.

steps.title: Optimize the area
steps.body: For positive w, both w and w + 3 increase with w. The greatest feasible width 10 gives length 13 and area 130.

steps.title: Check feasibility
steps.body: The perimeter is 2(10) + 2(13) = 46. Width 11 would require perimeter 50.

resolution.takeaway: Solve the constraint first, then evaluate the objective at the justified extreme.

beats.purpose: Consolidate translation, transformation, endpoint, feasibility, and optimization safeguards.
beats.expectedRealization: A reliable solution proves the feasible set before selecting and checking an extreme.
beats.transitionIn: Bins, tickets, walls, water, times, donations, and rectangles used the same safeguards. Gather them into one routine.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable constraint-and-optimization routine? Select all four.

options.text: Translate every limit and keep the variable's meaning and domain visible.
Use matched operations, reversing direction after multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Mark the feasible set with correct open or closed endpoints and integer restrictions.
Choose the requested extreme from the feasible set and check nearby boundary values.

response.feedback: Each action protects a different part of the argument.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—translate, solve carefully, mark feasibility, then optimize and check.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are needed: constraints define the set, transformations preserve it, endpoints describe it, and optimization selects from it.

visual.ariaLabel: Four stages of solving and optimizing under constraints

steps.title: Keep the proof in order
steps.body: A minimum or maximum is justified only after every constraint and domain restriction has identified the values allowed to compete.

resolution.takeaway: Feasible first; extreme second; check the boundary and its neighbor.

beats.purpose: Extend the feasible-set idea to two varying quantities without claiming an unmapped successor.
beats.expectedRealization: With two variables, a constraint can describe many feasible pairs rather than an interval of single values.
beats.transitionIn: One number line was enough when only x varied. Now let two choices share one limit.
beats.prompt: A snack cart can carry at most 30 items split between fruit cups f and sandwiches s. What might the feasible pairs look like, and where would you search if profit depended differently on f and s?
beats.takeaway: When two quantities vary, constraints create a region of feasible pairs, and an optimum must still come from inside that region.

notes: Design: the opening changes the familiar equality x + 7 = 18 into the capacity inequality x + 7 ≤ 18, exposing a solution interval. The central tension is that endpoint and direction choices change which values are feasible. With no named successor, the closing extends the idea to a two-variable feasible region.

Beat outline: capacity puzzle -> translate at most -> inspect endpoints -> transform a positive inequality -> discover negative reversal -> name feasible intervals -> generated budget anchor -> separate feasibility from optimization -> authentic block-wall transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> two-variable hook.
The number-line primitive is a generic, serializable, accessible static visual. Attempt states remain unshaded whenever shading would reveal an answer; completed intervals appear only in resolutions.

The block-wall animation appears only after submission. Its four learner prompts match the scene's four declared states, so the tempting 350-block arrangement and the 353-block optimum are revealed at the appropriate time.
All generated answers were verified algebraically and independently through boundary checks, option audits, or enumeration. The lesson remains draft pending human pedagogical review.
